Why now? We have not come forward in the past with an obligation to improve the infrastructure. Why now? It is essential because people are looking for some kind of hope. It is one initiative that everybody agrees on, except for the federal government.
I can just see it. What a psychological lift it would be if we began to invest in infrastructure. It would create
63,000	new jobs every year for five years. I can hear the hum of activity across the country. Not only would it be an investment but it would be a psychological lift for people. These people would be back to work, not on a make-work job creation project, but on a real investment, something that when we were finished, is there and ready for the new prosperity that this government has said is coming soon.
I certainly hope it comes, but when it does come, after the Tories are gone, we have to be prepared to deal with it. We will only be prepared if we have the infrastructure to deal with it. People say it is going to be too costly. FCM says it will cost $400 million over five years. That is what it will add to the deficit. If we put 63,000 people back to work every year for five years, they will become taxpayers. They will become involved in the economy of the country. It is not too much to pay.
What are other countries doing? One of President Clinton's major platforms during the election campaign was an investment in infrastructure. The Japanese are investing $1 trillion over a 10-year period. Their debt is just fine, thank you. In fact there is no debt at all.
What does this government say? We have to get the fundamentals right before we proceed, before we spend any more money. God forbid. I was a teacher for 28 years. If anybody cannot get the fundamentals right in eight years, we have problems. Eventually we have to tell the student, in this case the government, it has failed, no more. It has failed and it does not have time to get the fundamentals right.
In maintenance versus reconstruction, investment is important. The longer one delays, the greater the cost. It is 10 times more costly to reconstruct than to maintain. What costs $15 billion now will cost $150 billion in 10 years. We will not be able to afford it then.
Everybody is at the ready. All we require is the government. Every municipality in this country is saying:
"Just give us the go ahead". The projects are in place. The engineering is all set to go. In my municipality of Sault Ste. Marie it takes $15 million every year just for the maintenance of the infrastructure.
I beg the government to come onside and as an appropriate parting gift to the member for Regina- Lumsden join with everybody in this country and say yes to this motion.

Mr. Speaker, it is with great pleasure that I rise today to speak to the motion moved by my honorable friend, Motion M-281 which reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should join with provincial government to establish a tri-level program for the funding of infrastructure improvements, including improvements to sewage and water treatment facilities, road and bridge repair and the construction of grade separation at railway crossings.
We cannot expect that a federal contribution for repairs to infrastructures will make workers more competitive. This is not a panacea. It is not going to solve all our problems. It is not just a way to create jobs, because these jobs will be a relatively short-term proposition. The main purpose is to help the provinces and municipalities that desperately need to repair their infrastructure. Today, those repairs would cost about $20 billion, according to the statistics of the Federation of Canadian Municipalities. Five or six years ago, it was about half-not quite $10 billion. We have nothing to gain by delaying repairs to Canadian infrastructure.
It is not going to get any cheaper. This may seem incredible, but as the hon. member said earlier, it costs ten times as much to rebuild an infrastructure as it does to repair one. Ten times. Today, this is a Canada-wide problem. Across Canada, municipal and provincial authorities are asking us to help them repair their infrastructures.
It is a pleasure to see the former mayor of Ville d'Anjou in the House. In fact, not many people know he is the former mayor of Ville d'Anjou. His role is not that of a former mayor. He is now Minister of Transport, and I am sure that when the Minister of Transport was just a mayor, his people would ask him: Could you help us do

something about the infrastructure in our town? I am sure that as a responsible mayor, the minister would say: In that case, we need federal assistance. We need the federal government. Today, however, the mayor is the Minister of Transport, and as such will share the responsibility for implementing a highway improvement program across Canada. He should help us set priorities. He should also support Motion M-281 presented by my hon. friend, because when he was mayor, his people trusted him to help them.
Today, his perception is no longer that of a mayor but of a Minister of Transport, and as Minister of Transport, he should have a very good grasp of what is involved because of his experience as mayor. I am very pleased he is here tonight, although it is nearly 9.30 p.m., and I know he is dedicated because he is listening very carefully.
This motion is a good thing for Canada, at a time when we see a certain tendency by the government to dump its responsibilities on to the provinces and municipalities.
I think this is the right time to support a private member's motion, even if it happens to be a motion by an opposition member, because it reflects the most elementary and most important aspect of a bill, and I am referring to common sense. It made sense to U.S. President Clinton, who said in one of his election speeches that he would provide for repairs to U.S. infrastructure.
I am sure the government, whether it is this government or the next one-it will probably be an NDP government, or maybe another government, who knows, it might be a Liberal government-but sooner or later, it will have to deal with the problem of our infrastructure. If it is a New Democratic government, Mr. Speaker-I see I have your attention-it will be sooner rather than later. The problem is that every time a New Democratic government comes to power and opens the treasury to see what is inside, there was always either a Conservative government, as in Saskatchewan, or a Social Credit government, as in British Columbia, or a Liberal government-dare I mention it-as in Ontario, which had left the cupboard bare.
Private Members' Business
Even if the cupboard is bare, the problem still has to be dealt with, which is what they did in British Columbia, Saskatchewan and Ontario.
I know we will be blamed for not punishing people for the mistakes of the Liberals, the Conservatives and the Social Credit. I know they will say that, but the fact is, we have to do something about infrastructure. We cannot go on like this.
I think it is important to point out tonight that not many people said they wanted to vote against the hon. member's motion. They did not say they would vote against the motion. One Conservative member said it needed something more. One Liberal said: "We said this before. We already said this had to be done". Recently, another Conservative said: "It makes sense but I do not think now is the right time".
Good grief, if now is not the right time, then when is the right time? If their party cannot make the right decision, they should move over and let us make the right decisions. Come over here, and we will make the right decisions.
In concluding, I want to say that the hon. member's motion was not criticized by either the Liberals or the Conservatives. This goes to show there is a very real need to provide funding for infrastructure improvement. The benefits are threefold: First, for the environment, by cleaning up our waterways; second, for residential construction. People will still be able to own homes in locations with convenient access. Finally, there is a definite benefit for industry. Industries want to locate in places with excellent infrastructure.
It is really in our best interests to support a motion I see as a common sense motion, and the hon. member is to be commended for presenting it.
